title: Diwali Cracker Prices to Rise 15-20% as Sivakasi Production Falls and Labour Runs Short
excerpt: The Times of India puts this year's increase at 15-20%, and Sivakasi manufacturers say output is down about a quarter on a worker shortage.
body:
• Firecracker prices will be 15% to 20% higher this Diwali, The Times of India reported, squeezing the standard family cracker budget.
  • In Sivakasi, the industry's hub, one factory manager reported production down about 25% from last year and blamed a worker shortage.
  • Units that once employed 100 to 120 workers now run with 70 to 75, manufacturers in Sivakasi told reporters in late September.
  • Budget the same quantity and a family should expect to pay roughly a fifth more than last Diwali, or buy a fifth less for the same money.

Families buying firecrackers for Diwali will pay 15% to 20% more this year, The Times of India reported, as India's cracker industry heads into its peak season with less stock and fewer hands to make it. The increase lands on one of the festival's most price-sensitive purchases: a discretionary bag of sparklers, fountains and sky shots that many households trim first when budgets tighten.

Less production in Sivakasi

The pressure starts in Sivakasi, Tamil Nadu, the town that supplies most of India's fireworks. Firecracker units there stepped up operations ahead of Diwali to meet orders from across the country, but manufacturers and workers reported a decline in production caused by a shortage of labour and by regulatory restrictions, according to reporting from Sivakasi in late September. Kannan, a manager at Udhayraj Fireworks who has worked at the factory for 10 years, said production had dropped by about 25% compared with last year and that prices had gone up, with the worker shortage the main cause.

"Compared to last year, production has dropped by 25 per cent. Prices have gone up and, mainly, we have a huge worker shortage."

— Kannan, manager, Udhayraj Fireworks, via NewKerala

Kannan said his unit now employs around 70 to 75 people, down from 100 to 120 earlier, as other factories opening nearby compete for the same workers. The unit makes flower pots, wheels, fancy items and multi-shot and single-shot fireworks, and orders from northern India have helped, even though overall orders remain lower than last year.

The workers behind the price

For Sivakasi's workforce, slower production is not an abstraction. Muthulakshmi, who has worked in the industry for 22 years, told reporters the fireworks trade is the only livelihood available in and around her village, and that the slowdown has hit household spending on food and children's education. Diwali earnings, including the seasonal bonus, depend on how fast units can work in the final weeks — the same weeks when scarcity is pushing retail prices up.

What it means for buyers, including the diaspora

For shoppers in India, the arithmetic is simple: the same assortment costs 15% to 20% more, so families will either spend more or burst less. For diaspora households celebrating in the United States, the Sivakasi squeeze matters mainly through imported stock at Indian grocery and festival stores, where supply is thinner and local fireworks rules vary by state and city — check your local rules before buying, and expect popular items to sell out earlier than usual this year.

What to watch

Traders will be watching whether last-minute demand holds up at the higher prices, and whether the labour shortage eases after the festival. If production stays a quarter below last year's level, this Diwali's increase may not be a one-off.
